FDE-Bench: Evaluating
End-to-End Delivery from Underspecified
Real-World Business Requests
Huaiming Li1, ∗, Can Huang2, ∗, Chufan Wu1, Danyu Liu1, Xiaomin Yuan1, Qinze Li1, Yui Lo1,
Wenhui Bai1, Qianlong Wang1, Zengle Ge1, Xiyu Yan1, Yuheng Cheng3, Jinhui Ren4,
Guokai Chen4, Jiaqun Liu5, Haoran Li6, Qianhui Liu7, Annan Li1, Jianmin Wu1, Dawei Yin1,
Dou Shen1, †
1 FM Agent Team, Baidu AI Cloud
2 Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications
3 The Chinese University of Hong Kong
4 Tsinghua University
5 Peking University
6 University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences
7 Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Real-world business requests often leave key requirements unstated because frontline practitioners struggle
to articulate rules they know from experience.
Forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) must elicit these
requirements through dialogue and iteratively optimize solutions until they meet customer acceptance
criteria.
Existing optimization benchmarks typically start from explicit objectives, while clarification
benchmarks often introduce information gaps into existing tasks.
We introduce FDE-Bench, the first
benchmark built from real customer projects to evaluate agents on end-to-end delivery tasks that require
interactive requirement clarification and iterative optimization. Its 49 cases span combinatorial optimization
and machine learning. Clarification targets are distilled from discussions between frontline practitioners and
FDEs. Agents elicit missing requirements from a simulated customer, and case-specific evaluators assess final
artifacts against acceptance criteria using customer-accepted FDE solutions as quality references. Across 18
agent configurations, the highest mean delivery score is only 0.5510, compared with an FDE reference of
1.0. The highest delivery success rate (DSR), defined as the fraction of planned runs reaching this reference,
is only 6.12%. These results show that reliable FDE-level end-to-end delivery remains out of reach for the
evaluated agents on underspecified real-world business tasks. The benchmark project page is available at
baidubce.github.io/FM-Agent/FDE-Bench.
1 Introduction
In real customer projects, frontline practitioners often rely on business rules learned through experience but
struggle to make them explicit in their requests [1]. Forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) must elicit these tacit
requirements through dialogue and iteratively optimize solutions until they meet the customer’s acceptance
criteria [2]. Figure 1(a) illustrates a warehouse request to keep each stack to “one product type” where
possible while avoiding unnecessary stock moves. The request leaves implicit that different batches of the
same product (SKU) also count as mixed. Grouping only by SKU can therefore leave mixed stacks under the
customer’s criterion. After clarifying this rule, the agent must still iteratively refine storage assignments and
moves to meet the delivery requirements.
Representative benchmarks do not yet fully capture this challenge.
Optimization benchmarks such as
HeuriGym [3] and Frontier-Eng [4] provide explicit objectives and constraints, leaving requirement acquisition
outside their scope. ClarEval [5] perturbs programming instructions to create omissions and ambiguities,
while HIL-Bench [6] introduces human-validated blockers requiring interaction in coding and SQL tasks.
Their information gaps are constructed within predefined tasks; we instead ask whether agents can elicit
requirements grounded in frontline practitioners’ experience and iteratively optimize solutions to meet real
customers’ delivery standards.
We introduce FDE-Bench, a benchmark of 49 cases from real customer projects for evaluating agents from
requirement clarification through iterative optimization to final delivery. As summarized in Figure 1(b), the

Figure 1 | FDE-Bench: motivation and coverage. (a) Clarifying mixing rules guides iterative warehouse

cases cover 29 combinatorial-optimization and 20 machine-learning tasks across diverse business settings.
Each case links the original request and business data, requirements distilled from frontline practitioner–FDE
discussions, and a customer-accepted FDE solution. Agents clarify requirements with a simulated customer,
then iteratively execute and improve their solutions. After submission, case-specific evaluators assess final
artifacts against the project’s acceptance criteria, using the accepted FDE solution as the quality reference.
Separate clarification scores measure how well agents’ questions cover the annotated requirements. Since
performance depends on both the model and its scaffold [7], we build an extensible evaluation harness to
compare different configurations under a shared protocol.
We evaluate 18 agent configurations spanning seven model families and six agent scaffolds. Across configurations,
the highest mean delivery score is only 0.5510 against a customer-accepted FDE reference of 1.0. The highest
delivery success rate (DSR)—the fraction of planned runs reaching that reference—is only 6.12%. Broader
requirement coverage in agents’ questions is associated with higher delivery quality. Paired information
comparisons show higher scores with required clarification than with no customer answers, but even complete
business information leaves all compared configurations below the FDE reference on average. These results
expose gaps in both requirement acquisition and solution optimization.
Our contributions are:
• A benchmark for end-to-end FDE delivery. FDE-Bench is the first benchmark to couple interactive
requirement clarification with iterative optimization on real customer projects, using customer-accepted
FDE solutions as delivery references.
• An extensible evaluation harness. Backend adapters support new models and agent scaffolds; a shared
protocol records interactions and evaluates submitted artifacts, with separate measures of requirement
coverage and delivery quality.
• A systematic study of current agents. Across 18 configurations, we analyze representative delivery
failures and the association between requirement coverage and delivery quality. Information ablations show
that complete business information alone does not close the delivery gap.
2 Related Work
Optimization modeling and search. NL4Opt and OptiMUS study natural-language optimization modeling,
while OptiBench and OptMATH provide data for evaluating or training modeling systems [8–11]. MIPLIB-NL
extends evaluation to industrial-scale mixed-integer problems [12]. CO-Bench, HeuriGym, and ALE-Bench
2


--- Page 3 ---
evaluate iterative algorithm search and optimization [3, 13, 14], while ORAgentBench and Opti-Agent-Bench
extend evaluation to workflows involving problem formulation, file inspection, and execution [15, 16]. These
works primarily assess how agents formulate and solve given optimization tasks. FDE-Bench additionally
evaluates whether agents can elicit unstated business requirements through customer interaction and use
them to guide optimization.
Clarification and interactive agents. MINT evaluates multi-turn tool use with language feedback, while
τ-bench studies customer interaction and policy compliance in API-based service tasks [17, 18]. CLAMBER
focuses on identifying ambiguous information needs and generating clarifying questions [19]. HIL-Bench
introduces blockers into coding and SQL tasks, while ClarEval injects ambiguities into programming instructions
[5, 6]. Ambig-SWE evaluates clarification in software tasks [20], while Pan et al. [21] study code generation
with interactive feedback. SWE-RPG diagnoses implicit-requirement recovery from coding trajectories but
does not evaluate interactive user feedback [22]. FDE-Bench grounds clarification targets in discussions
between frontline practitioners and FDEs from real customer projects, then evaluates delivery quality after
agents clarify requirements and iteratively optimize their solutions.
Executable evaluation and expert references. SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench use executable verifica-
tion to assess software and command-line tasks [23, 24]. Frontier-Eng and EngDesign evaluate engineering
solutions through task-specific scoring or simulation [4, 25]. MLE-bench measures machine-learning engineer-
ing performance, while RE-Bench compares agents with human experts on ML research engineering tasks
[26, 27]. FDE-Bench also uses executable evaluation and reference solutions. Its distinguishing feature is
that the initial request, clarification targets, and customer-accepted FDE reference originate from the same
customer project. Agents must elicit initially unstated requirements and optimize their deliverables against
that project’s acceptance criteria. Appendix A.1 provides a comparison with representative benchmarks.
3 FDE-Bench: Tasks and Construction
3.1 FDE Delivery Workflow
Each case draws on the FDE delivery workflow of a real customer project (Figure 2). Frontline practitioners
provide an underspecified business request and business data. Through discussion, the FDE elicits business
rules and acceptance criteria, then iteratively optimizes a solution until customer acceptance. The initial
request and data, project discussions, and accepted FDE solution from the same project supply task inputs,
requirement annotations, and delivery references, respectively. The original discussion transcripts remain
hidden from evaluated agents.
3.2 Benchmark Construction Pipeline
Prepare task inputs.
The initial request and business data are de-identified with agent assistance and
reviewed by an FDE. The process preserves the request’s original meaning and level of detail, applies
replacements consistently across related files, and retains numerical relationships and constraints needed for
execution and evaluation. The visible inputs are instruction.md and data/; the de-identification agent does
not decide requirements or acceptance criteria.
Distill requirements.
The FDE responsible for the original delivery annotates requirements established
in the customer–FDE discussions. We store complete business context in information.md and clarification
targets in gt.json. A target is retained only if it cannot be resolved from the initial request and visible data,
and its resolution can affect feasibility, the objective or target value, or customer acceptance. Examples
include the meaning of a data field, the scope of a constraint, and the convention used to measure an objective.
Each annotation records the requirement and the information to clarify, without prescribing question wording
or dialogue order. The 49 cases contain 266 targets, or 5.43 per case on average.
Establish delivery evaluation.
Complete requirements and project acceptance criteria are translated
into a case-specific evaluator that checks the artifact schema, hard constraints, and case-defined quality. The
customer-accepted FDE deliverable supplies the reference, normalized to 1.0. This is an achieved project

requirements, case-specific evaluation, and a reviewed case package.
standard rather than a claim of global optimality; different algorithms are therefore judged against a common
set of requirements.
Human review and selection.
Reviewers run each FDE reference solution with its evaluator and check
that the evaluation matches the documented business requirements and acceptance criteria. They also review
the FDE annotations using common criteria across cases, checking targets against the evaluator and reference
artifact, removing duplicates, and confirming that each target has a documented customer answer. Cases with
incomplete materials or inconsistent checks are excluded. To select projects involving sustained delivery work,
we retain those that required more than one month of FDE effort on clarification and iterative optimization
before customer acceptance. Reviewers select cases across computational task types and business settings to
ensure coverage.
3.3 Task Coverage and Specification
The release contains 29 combinatorial-optimization and 20 machine-learning cases, spanning manufacturing,
logistics, energy, retail, finance, and engineering settings. Primary computational subtypes are listed in the
case inventory; scenario tags can overlap and are not mutually exclusive counts.
We represent each case as C = (u, D, I, G, E), comprising the initial request u, business data D, complete
business-information file I, clarification targets G, and case-specific evaluator E. Each released case package
also includes an FDE reference deliverable and its reference quality, an execution environment, and metadata.
Under the main condition, Interact-Req, only u and D are initially exposed in the solving workspace; I, G,
E, and the reference deliverable remain outside it. Section 4 specifies how agents interact with the simulated
customer and how their submitted artifacts and clarification questions are evaluated.
4 Evaluation Protocol
FDE-Bench evaluates two outputs of each run: the submitted solution file (the artifact) and the interaction log.
Case-specific evaluators score delivery, while a separate judge panel assesses clarification coverage (Figure 3).
Section 5.4 compares the main condition, Interact-Req, with no-answer and full-information conditions.

After submission, hidden evaluation extracts and scores artifacts against FDE references without online feedback;

4.1 Evaluation Procedure
Customer interaction.
Agents query a simulated customer for business information. The customer uses
the request u, complete business information I, and dialogue history to answer, without access to clarification
targets G. We use GLM-5.3 with a fixed prompt and record exchanges. Benchmark prompts and the
native-tool, callback, and text-exchange interfaces are provided with the benchmark.
Solving and submission.
The Interact-Req prompt instructs agents to elicit missing information before
implementation, continuing until they consider the information sufficient. Within the execution budget and
interaction limits, agents choose their questions, implement a candidate solution, execute it locally, inspect
the resulting files and diagnostics, and repeatedly revise and re-execute the solution. They submit the final
artifact only after this local optimization loop. The main campaign allows 43,200 seconds (12 hours) per
solving run, including interaction, and at most 30 clarification rounds with no separate question-count cap.
The hidden evaluator and artifact extractor run only after submission and provide no score or evaluator
feedback during this loop.
Extraction and case evaluation.
After submission, extractors convert artifacts into the case evaluator’s
input format while preserving the agent’s solution and decisions. The evaluator checks the case’s hard
constraints. Violations receive a delivery score of zero; otherwise, it computes case-defined quality and
normalizes it to the customer-accepted FDE reference, which scores 1.0. Up to five models—GLM-5.2,
Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Gemini-3.6-Flash, and Grok-4.5—extract the artifact for scoring by the
same case evaluator. Remaining routes are skipped once three scores agree after rounding to four decimal
places. A score is recorded when at least three routes agree. The validity outcome is taken from an evaluation
supporting that score; this model-panel design is related to prior work on LLM-assisted evaluation [28, 29].
Requirement coverage.
We split recorded questions into units and use the same five models to assess
coverage of G. For each requirement, judges independently assess whether answering at least one question
would reveal it. Judges receive the requirement and numbered questions, but not customer answers or
requirement-category metadata. Coverage is accepted when at least three of five judgments agree (≥3/5);
otherwise the requirement is uncovered.
4.2 Evaluation Metrics
FDE tasks require agents to elicit implicit business requirements and turn them into a deliverable that meets
the customer’s standard. We measure clarification and delivery separately to examine whether effective
requirement acquisition translates into successful delivery.
Delivery metrics.
In the main evaluation, each configuration runs three times on each of 49 cases. Quality
first averages the three delivery scores within each case, then averages across cases with equal weight. Delivery
Success Rate (DSR) is the fraction of the 147 runs reaching the FDE reference. Let sir denote the delivery
score for repeat r of case i. We define
Quality = 1

Following the pass@k framing in code-generation evaluation [30], we also report pass@3 and pass^3: the
fractions of cases with at least one and all three valid runs, respectively. These measure validity across
repeated runs; DSR measures attainment of the FDE reference.
Clarification metrics.
Missing business requirements can lead an agent to solve the wrong problem. Recall
(R) measures how fully its questions cover the reference requirements, while Precision (P) measures how
focused the questions are on those requirements. Their harmonic mean, Ask-F1, rewards broad coverage with
focused questioning, following the standard precision–recall terminology in information retrieval [31]. For
each run, let Gcov ⊆G denote covered requirements, Q the set of question-unit indices, and Qrel ⊆Q the
indices matched to at least one covered requirement. These three primary metrics are
R = |Gcov|
|G| ,
P = |Qrel|
|Q| ,
Ask-F1 = 2PR
P + R.
Recall is question coverage: it measures whether a question could elicit a reference requirement, not whether
the customer stated it or the agent used it; questions matching multiple requirements count once.
Efficient clarification should elicit business requirements with few customer exchanges and limited question
burden. First-turn coverage (KQC1) measures how much agents cover in the initial exchange, while average
turns to clarify (ATC) measures how early they address the requirements eventually covered. Unmatched-
question count (Redund.) captures the absolute number of questions unmatched to covered requirements.
Interpreted alongside Recall, these diagnostics characterize the trade-off between requirement coverage and
interaction effort. Let Gcov,1 ⊆G denote requirements covered in the first interaction turn, and G⋆
cov ⊆Gcov
those with a recorded matching question and turn. For each requirement g ∈G⋆
cov, let tg be its first covering
turn, counting from 1. We define

Clarification metrics are computed per run and averaged over runs for which each metric is defined.
4.3 Evaluation Reliability
Two human experts independently audited stratified samples of retained traces, covering 1,303 simulated-
customer answers, 120 artifact extractions, and 120 clarification items across all 18 configurations. Sampling
procedures, confidence intervals, and full audit results are provided in Appendix A.8. For answer grounding,
experts A and B marked 95.93% and 90.48% of answers as supported, respectively; their support labels agreed
on 92.10% of records (Cohen’s κ = 0.385 [32]). For extraction fidelity, on a sample enriched for runs with
extraction issues, they judged 93.33% and 91.00% of assessable extractions faithful to the submitted artifacts,
respectively, with 91.67% three-category agreement (Cohen’s κ = 0.7656). For clarification coverage, the model
panel agreed with expert A on 94.74% (κ = 0.8947) and with B on 93.33% (κ = 0.8667), excluding uncertain
labels. These results support the reliability of the evaluation pipeline on the audited subsets; the extraction
κ specifically measures expert-label agreement, rather than extractor accuracy against an adjudicated gold
standard. These checks reduce but do not eliminate extraction-related score risk.
5 Experiments
We evaluate 18 agent systems and ask three questions. RQ1 (§5.2): how close do agents come to the accepted
FDE deliverable? RQ2 (§5.3): which clarification behaviors distinguish stronger systems? RQ3 (§5.4): how
does delivery quality change with access to business information?
5.1 Experimental Setup
We evaluate scaffold–model systems: general scaffolds opencode and openhands, each with seven models
(GPT-6-Astra, GLM-5.3, Qwen3.8-Max, Grok-4.6, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi-K3, Gemini-3.1-Pro), and four
native pairs (codex, deepseek-harness, kimi, gemini). All main runs use Interact-Req with a fixed simulated
6


--- Page 7 ---
customer, a 12-hour budget, and at most 30 clarification rounds; each system solves each of 49 cases three
times. Paired contrasts use two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests [33] on case means with Holm correction [34].
Settings and bootstrap intervals are reported with the released results.

FDE-level delivery remains rare.
Across the 18 systems, the highest mean Quality is only 0.5510 (codex
+ GPT-6-Astra), and the highest DSR is 6.12% (Table 1). Only 8 of 49 cases have any reference-level run,
and in 23 the best system averages below 0.8. Four systems, including all three Gemini-3.1-Pro systems, reach
the reference in none of their 147 runs, and no ML run reaches it in any system.
Validity varies across repeated runs.
Across systems, 85.7–95.9% of cases have at least one valid repeat
among three attempts (pass@3). However, pass^3 trails pass@3 for every system by 8.2–38.8 percentage
points (mean 23.0): for a typical system, 23% of cases are valid in some runs but not in all three. Of the 548
zero-score runs, 78.5% record a constraint or feasibility violation and 1.5% a schema error (Appendix A.7):
agents submit well-formed artifacts that break business rules.
Runtime and case difficulty.
Across systems, mean run time ranges from 0.3 to 5.5 hours, with no
significant association with Quality (Spearman ρ = 0.18, p = 0.47) [35]. Case-level Quality rankings are
similar across systems (mean pairwise Spearman ρ = 0.71).
The model matters more than the scaffold.
With the scaffold fixed, Quality spans 0.159 across models
on opencode and 0.118 on openhands; with the model fixed, the two general scaffolds differ by at most 0.032
for six models (Gemini-3.1-Pro: 0.387 vs. 0.457). Native scaffolds add 0.005 and 0.017 for GPT-6-Astra and
DeepSeek-V4-Pro, while gemini trails openhands by 0.053.

Average turns to clarify is 1.01–1.16, and
first-turn coverage is 91–99% of final Recall. Under Interact-Req’s instruction to clarify before implementation,
most covered requirements are addressed in the initial exchange.
More questions do not consistently improve delivery.
Unmatched-question count correlates with DSR
(ρ = 0.75, Holm p = 0.006): systems that ask more cover more requirements and also ask more unmatched
questions. On the five most requirement-dense cases, mandatory rather than optional clarification raises
question count for all eight tested systems and Recall for seven, but Quality for only five; the changes range
from −0.125 to +0.196 and none is significant (Holm p ≥0.50).
Case study: asking about a rule does not ensure compliance.
In case 10 (retail replenishment),
opencode + GPT-6-Astra asks whether same-city stock must be used before supplier purchases. Its local
validator reports pass, but the submitted plan purchases an item from a supplier while the local warehouse
still holds 327 units. The hidden evaluator identifies violations of this priority rule at eight stores, and the
run receives Quality 0 (Appendix A.7). This run illustrates a gap between asking about a business rule and
enforcing it in the final deliverable.

Figure 5 | Oracle information coverage. Codex + GPT-6-Astra receives nested answer subsets; panels (a)–(d)
show four cases and (e) their macro mean.
Oracle returns are nonlinear and case-dependent. We give codex + GPT-6-Astra nested random subsets of the
registered answers on four cases, without interaction. At 100% coverage, agents receive all registered answers,
not the complete business-information file used by Full. Mean Quality rises from 0.059 at 0% coverage to
0.352 at 50% and 0.869 at 100%; the last quarter of answers yields half of the gain. Case 38 scores zero in
every run up to 50% coverage and 0.965 at full coverage, and at intermediate coverage cases 09 and 38 obtain
a nonzero score in one of three repeats and score zero in the others (Figure 5). A few unresolved requirements
can void an otherwise reasonable solution, which is consistent with RQ1: the highest Recall is 84.7%, yet no
system exceeds 6.12% DSR.
6 Conclusion
We introduced FDE-Bench to evaluate agents’ end-to-end delivery from underspecified real-world business
requests. Its 49 cases use customer-accepted FDE solutions as delivery references. Across 18 configurations, the
highest mean Quality is only 0.5510 against an FDE reference of 1.0. The highest delivery success rate is only
6.12%. Broader requirement coverage is associated with higher delivery quality, but even complete business
information leaves all compared configurations below the FDE reference on average. Reliable FDE-level
delivery therefore requires progress in both requirement clarification and solution optimization. FDE-Bench
provides a shared testbed for comparing new agent systems and examining whether better requirement
elicitation translates into better delivery.
7 Limitations and Future Work
FDE-Bench evaluates delivery with stable business requirements and fixed datasets. The simulated customer
does not revise its requirements in response to intermediate solutions, whereas real customers may reveal or
change expectations during development [2]. The benchmark therefore does not yet assess agents’ ability to
maintain delivery quality as production data and customer requirements evolve. Coverage is limited to 49
real customer projects in combinatorial optimization and machine learning. These cases do not cover all FDE
settings.
We plan to expand FDE-Bench with additional real customer projects across more domains, including scientific
and engineering applications. Selection will prioritize task types and business settings that are underrepresented
in the current release. New cases will undergo the same requirement review and reference-solution checks.
Future evaluations should incorporate continuously updated production data, evolving requirements, and
human customers, testing both sustained delivery quality and the realism of simulated interactions. Evaluation
in these settings should assess successive deliverables against the customer’s current acceptance criteria and
track how agents respond to requirement changes.

A.1 Benchmark comparison
Table 3 compares FDE-Bench with representative benchmarks and systems (Section 2).
Requirements
denotes implicit business requirements annotated from customer–engineer discussions in real delivery projects.
Reference denotes a customer-accepted project solution used as a delivery-quality baseline. These definitions
concern the provenance of the requirements and reference; RE-Bench, for example, provides human expert
comparisons and reference solutions, but not customer-accepted project deliverables.

Clarification points.
A clarification point is retained only if (i) it cannot be resolved from the agent-visible
request and data, (ii) the customer’s answer can change a feasible decision, the objective, or the evaluator’s
acceptance judgment, and (iii) the answer can be stated as a fact, rule, or convention that the evaluator
applies to the artifact. Implementation preferences, facts visible in the workspace, and questions about the
agent’s method are excluded.
Splitting and merging.
A candidate is split when two answers change different decisions or evaluator
checks, e.g., the error metric, which changes the score, and the valid value range, which changes whether the
artifact is accepted. Paraphrases and examples of the same decision are merged into one point. Table 5 lists
boundary cases.
Table 5 | Boundary examples for clarification points.
Candidate
Decision
Reason
“Is error MAE or relative error?”
Keep as one valid point
Changes the evaluator’s scoring
convention.
“Does same-city supplier precedence override
cost minimization?”
Keep as one valid point
Changes a routing/fulfillment rule
and can change feasibility.
“Are out-of-range predictions rejected?”
Keep as one valid point
Changes a hard constraint.
“What Python library should I use?”
Exclude
Implementation choice is not
scored.
“How many rows are in the visible CSV?”
Exclude
The fact is already observable to
the agent.
“Which metric and which value range are
required?”
Split into two points
Metric changes the score; range
changes acceptance.
“Should same-city orders precede transfers, and
should they be grouped?”
Merge when the evaluator has
one precedence rule; split
otherwise
The split is determined by
independent counterfactual
answers, not punctuation.

--- Page 18 ---
Registry fields.
Each point in gt.json has a key and four fields: the requirement description, issue
type (missing, ambiguous, invalidated, or conflicting), content domain (scoring convention, constraint rule,
computation convention, or data semantics), and rule source (null if none).
Review protocol.
The FDE responsible for each original delivery annotated the requirements established in
the customer–FDE discussions. A second review applied the same criteria against the evaluator and reference
artifact, removed duplicates, and confirmed that each point had a customer answer; disagreements were
resolved against the evaluator code.
A.3 Metrics and runtime settings
Score selection.
Up to five extraction routes score each artifact, with remaining routes skipped once
three scores agree after rounding to four decimal places. Extractions without source provenance are rejected;
majority agreement alone does not prove that every decision was preserved (Appendix A.8). Without a
majority, the score is unavailable.
Aggregation.
A run is valid when its artifact satisfies the case’s hard constraints (Table 4); pass@3 and
pass^3 count valid repeats. Zero scores and invalid runs are included in Quality. Each main configuration
contributes three scored runs on each of 49 cases, with all 147 runs included in DSR (Section 4.2). All ablation
runs also have numeric scores. Clarification metrics are never imputed, and runtime, tool calls, and cost are
not part of any delivery metric.
Question units.
Agent messages are split at question marks into question units; a message without a
question mark counts as one unit. Turn indices come from the interaction log.
Coverage judgments.
Judges also receive annotated trigger examples as matching hints. Merely touching
a requirement’s topic does not count as coverage.
A covered point’s matched questions are those cited by the agreeing judges, and Precision counts distinct
matched questions.
Undefined values.
With no recorded questions, Precision and Ask-F1 are undefined and Recall is zero. If
every judgment in a run fails, all three metrics are unavailable; each metric is averaged only over runs where
it is defined.
Runtime.
Each solving run has 43,200 seconds, including interaction, and at most 30 clarification rounds,
with no cap on the number of questions or on cumulative tokens. OpenHands runs at most 200 agent steps
(max_iterations); these steps are distinct from customer exchanges. OpenCode passes a per-call output limit
of 131,072 tokens with a 1,000,000-token context. The native CLIs use SDK or provider defaults. OpenCode
sets neither temperature nor reasoning effort, and no run overrides the temperature. Exact runner, scaffold,
and dependency pins are provided with the artifact; the controls above are the settings relevant to interpreting
the experiments.
A.4 Full results
Entries are means with 95% case-bootstrap intervals (2,000 resamples, seed 12345), following the bootstrap
framework of Efron [36].
Delivery metrics.
Table 6(a) gives delivery results with intervals. Quality is case-macro and DSR is
run-level; pass@3 and pass^3 are case-level (Section 4.2). Every pair of unpaired Quality intervals overlaps,
because the intervals carry the variance between cases. Paired by case, the systems form two groups. The 12
systems built on GPT-6-Astra, GLM-5.3, Qwen3.8-Max, Grok-4.6, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro score 0.499–0.551;
the three Kimi-K3 systems and Gemini-3.1-Pro under opencode and gemini score 0.387–0.420.
All 60
differences between the groups exclude zero under a paired case bootstrap, and none of the 76 differences
within a group does. All differences above 0.08 are resolved and none of 0.04 or less, so 49 cases separate
models but not scaffolds of the same model. The exception is openhands + Gemini-3.1-Pro (0.457), which
exceeds the other two Gemini-3.1-Pro systems by 0.053 and 0.070 (both resolved). DSR does not rank systems:
15 of the 18 DSR intervals include zero.

Clarification metrics.
Clarification metrics are run-level (Section 4.2; Table 6(b)). Across the 18 systems,
Spearman ρ between Recall and Quality is 0.83; after subtracting each model’s mean over its scaffolds, it
is −0.31 (p = 0.22). Moving a model from opencode to openhands raises Recall for six of seven models
(DeepSeek-V4-Pro: 55.1% to 65.2%) and Redund. for five (Qwen3.8-Max: 16.3 to 22.6), lowers Precision for
six, and lowers Quality for five, by at most 0.032. Scaffold changes that increase coverage do not consistently
improve Quality; the policy ablation also shows mixed Quality changes (Appendix A.6).
Compute.
Provider cost was available for 15 of 18 configurations and showed no detectable association
with Quality; detailed accounting is included with the artifact rather than repeated here.

hidden from agents and judges and are not used by the primary scorer.

scaffolds (81.2% and 85.4%) although its Missing Recall is 10–17 points below GPT-6-Astra; the Invalidated
and Conflicting columns rest on 8 and 4 cases. Within a case, the issue type does not decide which points
are covered. In the 29 cases with both Missing and Ambiguous points, 16 of 18 systems cover Ambiguous
points less often (mean gap 7.2 points), but the gap reverses in 12 of the 29 cases (95% case-bootstrap CI
[−3.8, 17.7]).
The content domain does. Pooled over runs, agents cover 72.6% of constraint-rule points, 64.8% of computation
conventions, 56.6% of scoring conventions, and 56.6% of data-semantics points, and constraint rules have the
highest Recall for 16 of 18 systems. Within the same case, constraint rules are covered 14.6 points more often
than data semantics (22 cases; CI [3.9, 25.0]) and 15.9 points more than computation conventions (22 cases;
[2.8, 28.9]); the gap to scoring conventions (+12.5, 26 cases) has an interval that includes zero. Agents ask
about stated business rules more than about how fields are read and how quantities are computed. Covering
a constraint rule also has the largest association with delivery: within the same system and case, runs that
cover a constraint-rule point score 0.059 higher than runs that do not (292 system–case–point cells with mixed
coverage; Wilcoxon p = 0.006), against 0.027–0.035 for the other domains.
Across systems, coverage of every domain tracks Quality equally (Spearman ρ = 0.81–0.83), and the two
groups of Appendix A.4 differ by 16.2–20.7 points in every domain. Table 10 gives the domain mix of each
model’s matched questions; a question matched to points of several domains is split equally among them.
GPT-6-Astra is the only model that directs more of its matched questions to scoring conventions (28.8%) than
to constraint rules (26.7%); DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Gemini-3.1-Pro, and Grok-4.6 direct 20.1–21.7% to scoring
conventions and 31.5–33.0% to constraint rules. Over the 18 systems, the scoring share correlates with
Quality (ρ = 0.61) and the constraint share with lower Quality (ρ = −0.60; Holm p = 0.028 for both over
four domains). Neither association is robust: the case-bootstrap 95% intervals include zero ([−0.07, 0.64] and
[−0.69, 0.08]), and without the three GPT-6-Astra systems the correlations fall to 0.38 (p = 0.16) and −0.32
(p = 0.24).
Table 8(b) instead correlates each case’s share of points of a type with its delivery, averaged over configurations,
across all 49 cases.
No Quality interval excludes zero, so the type mix of a case does not predict its difficulty. The positive
Invalidated–DSR association rests on eight cases.

A.6 Ablations
Scope.
The three-condition ablation uses a 20-case subset. The policy ablation uses the five cases in that
subset with the most clarification points; exact case IDs and registry counts are provided with the artifact.

∆req and ∆total are significant for all eight systems; ∆remain is significant for five. What interaction recovers
depends on how many requirements the system asks about; what remains does not. Over the eight systems,
∆req rises with Recall on the same 20 cases (Spearman ρ = 0.86, p = 0.007), while ∆remain has ρ = 0.00. The
two Kimi-K3 systems show the difference: with Recall of 60.4% and 60.7% and the same Interact-Req Quality
(0.369), the native kimi CLI reaches 0.718 under Full and opencode 0.449, so ∆remain is +0.349 and +0.079.
Clarification policy.
Both policies are run on the five policy cases with the eight ablation configurations
(15 runs per configuration and policy). Interact lets the agent decide whether to ask; Interact-Req requires
clarification before implementation. #Q counts question units, and ask rate is the share of runs with at least
one question.
Without the requirement, agents still ask in 80–100% of runs, but they ask fewer questions: requiring
clarification multiplies #Q by 1.4–3.0 in all eight systems. The added questions are worth less than the ones
agents ask on their own. Measured as the change in matched questions over the change in #Q, they match a
covered requirement at 13.5–45.8%, below the Interact Precision of the same system in all eight. Recall rises
in seven systems, but by at most 2.1 points per added question. Agents ask their most useful questions first.
Quality changes are mixed (Table 12(b)): no Holm-adjusted p is below 0.5.

Oracle answer coverage.
We selected four cases (09, 11, 17, and 38) and ran codex + GPT-6-Astra
without a clarification channel. We evaluate five target coverage levels, r ∈{0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1}, using nested
subsets of the registered answers and three repeats per case and level. The 0% level is run separately from
Hidden; the 100% level supplies the registered answers, not the complete information file used by Full.
Table 13 gives the values plotted in Figure 5; exact subset construction is provided with the artifact.
Answer coverage improves Quality overall, but the case-level trends are non-monotonic. Specific answers
matter more than the number of answers, which also explains the high variance at intermediate coverage
levels. The registered-answer endpoint differs from Full, and coverage of a blocking point is necessary but not
sufficient for correct implementation; the table therefore provides an information-sensitivity analysis rather
than a claim that more answers always improve delivery.

no Quality; all have a complete artifact and pipeline record. Table 14 groups the recorded error_info into

Zero scores belong to cases more than to systems. They occur in 33 of the 49 cases, and 7 cases account for
half of them. The five cases with the most zeros (21, 10, 13, 18, and 38) contribute 233 (42.5%); in each, 17 or
18 of the 18 systems score zero at least once, and in case 21, 17 systems score zero in all three repeats. Within
a system and case, clarification separates failing from passing repeats only slightly: in the 202 cells with both
zero and nonzero repeats, zero-score repeats have Recall 58.6% against 63.6% (lower in 89 cells, higher in
72; Wilcoxon p = 0.021) and ask as many questions (22.8 vs. 23.2). Seventy-two zeros (13.1%) reached the
runtime limit but still produced a scored artifact; 54 of them also record a constraint violation, so a timeout
does not by itself explain the zero.
Case study: case 10.
We trace one run of case 10 (retail replenishment; 17 days, 73 stores, 3,055 items;
opencode + GPT-6-Astra, Interact-Req, first repeat); Table 15(a) gives the evidence chain.
For example, at one affected store on 2025-03-13, the submitted plan purchased item ITEM_000092 from
SUPPLIER_DEFAULT despite a local-store balance of 0.0 and 327.0 units available in WH_LOCAL; the
same hard gate violation occurs across the eight stores, summarized in Table 15(b).
The run thus shows a rule that was asked about but not enforced.
A.8 Audits
Audit sample and tasks.
Two experts, Annotator A and Annotator B, independently labeled 120
clarification items (105 runs, 38 cases) and 120 extraction runs (43 cases), each sample covering all 18
configurations. Samples were drawn with fixed seeds, stratified by configuration and by coverage or recorded
issue. A clarification item asks whether answering at least one recorded question would reveal the reference
point (covered, uncovered, or uncertain).
An extraction run compares the submitted artifact with its
normalized form (CORRECT, INCORRECT, or NOT_ASSESSABLE); runs without a submitted result
file are NOT_ASSESSABLE.

JSON replenishment plan; internal store/warehouse transfers must be exhausted before

over timeliness and cost.

source precedence (“same-city stores and local warehouse →cross-city sources →supplier”)

Post-hoc audit of simulated-customer answers.
Annotators A and B labeled the sampled customer
answers for support by the case information and consistency with earlier turns (Table 16(a)). The audit
indicates that the simulator’s main weakness is cross-turn inconsistency rather than direct conflict with the
case.
Agreement and uncertainty.
Table 16(b) reports agreement and unweighted Cohen’s κ with 95% case-
cluster bootstrap intervals (5,000 resamples). Six clarification items that Annotator A marked uncertain are
excluded from comparisons involving A; extraction agreement retains all three categories.
The panel does not systematically inflate Recall: its disagreements with Annotator A are balanced between
covered and uncovered labels.
Extraction agreement and failures.
We audited the retained result.json and extractor records of all
2,646 main runs. Numeric votes have strong majority agreement, while the remaining non-numeric failures
are rare and are broken down by configuration in Table 17. Because the 120-run audit sample was enriched
for recorded extraction issues, we reweighted it to the population; the resulting estimated extraction accuracy
is 97.9%.
Overall extraction failure rates are low across configurations, and majority voting reduces the effect of
individual extractor disagreements on final scores.

A.9 Prompt templates and interaction interfaces
This section reproduces the benchmark prompts for the solving agent, simulated customer, extractor, and
judge, and the question–answer interfaces. They form the benchmark layer added to each scaffold; the
scaffolds’ own prompts are unchanged. Double-braced fields are filled at runtime. The listings below show the
exact shared and role-specific templates used in the benchmark, including the information boundaries and the
no-repair extraction contract. Scaffold-specific wrappers and exact field substitutions are released with the
artifact in analysis/prompt_templates/.
A.9.1 Solving-agent instructions
All conditions use the same base template. The request block is the heading ## The client’s request
followed by the complete instruction.md; the data list contains the sorted filenames directly under data/.
The workspace is the run’s solving directory. Only the condition block changes.
Shared agent template
You are an algorithm delivery engineer. A client has sent you a business request and some data files.
Your job: understand what they actually need, then build a working solution and deliver it.
## Working directory
{{workspace}}
Data files provided by the client:
{{data_files}}
Write all outputs to the working directory.
{{request_block}}
{{condition_block}}
## Delivering
Do the work -- do not merely describe how you would do it. The task is complete only
when the deliverable files exist in the working directory.
Produce whatever artifact the request calls for. The client did not specify a file
format -- infer what is appropriate from what they asked for.
Also write a short ‘NOTES.md‘ recording your key modelling decisions: what you
assumed, what you inferred from the data, and anything you were unsure about.
Hidden condition block
## Missing information
The request is written in the client’s own words. It will not spell out every
detail you need -- data conventions, units, edge-case handling and similar points
are often left implicit because the client considers them obvious.
There is no one available to answer questions. Where something cannot be
determined from the request or the data, make a reasonable assumption, proceed,
and record the assumption in ‘NOTES.md‘.
27


--- Page 28 ---
Interact condition block
## Missing information
The request is written in the client’s own words. It will not spell out every
detail you need -- data conventions, units, edge-case handling and similar points
are often left implicit because the client considers them obvious.
The client is reachable and expects to be consulted on requirements. If something
cannot be determined from the request or the data, ask them. You may ask more
than once, and at any point in the work.
When you ask, put the questions at the end of your reply under a heading
‘## Questions for the client‘, one question per line, and stop there -- the client
will answer in the next message. (Asking in plain prose also works; the heading
just makes the exchange cleaner.)
For anything you choose not to ask about, make a reasonable assumption, proceed,
and record the assumption in ‘NOTES.md‘.
Interact-Req condition block
## Missing information
The request is written in the client’s own words. It will not spell out every
detail you need -- data conventions, units, edge-case handling and similar points
are often left implicit because the client considers them obvious.
The client is reachable. Before writing any code, ask the client about anything
you need settled, and keep asking until you have what you need. Do not start
the work until then.
Ask about anything the request and the data do not settle. You may ask across
several rounds.
When you ask, put the questions at the end of your reply under a heading
‘## Questions for the client‘, one question per line, and stop there -- the client
will answer in the next message. (Asking in plain prose also works; the heading
just makes the exchange cleaner.)
Proceeding on an unconfirmed reading counts as a failure even if the guess
turns out right. Record in ‘NOTES.md‘ any assumption the client did not settle.
Full condition block
## Additional context
The client has already supplied the following details, covering the data
conventions, units and edge-case handling that the request itself leaves implicit:
{{information}}
There is no one available to answer further questions. Where something is still
undetermined, make a reasonable assumption, proceed, and record it in ‘NOTES.md‘.
28


--- Page 29 ---
Oracle answer-coverage condition block
## Missing information
The request is written in the client’s own words. It will not spell out every
detail you need -- data conventions, units, edge-case handling and similar points
are often left implicit because the client considers them obvious.
The client has already settled the following points for you:
{{answers}}
There is no one available to answer further questions. Where something still
cannot be determined from the request, the data, or the points above, make a
reasonable assumption, proceed, and record the assumption in ‘NOTES.md‘.
For Full, information is the complete business-information file. For the oracle experiment, answers is the
selected answer text, rendered as bullets in registry order, or (none) for zero coverage. The nested subset
selection is specified in Appendix A.6; requirement identifiers and type labels are not inserted into the oracle
prompt.
A.9.2 Simulated-customer messages
The customer uses GLM-5.3 and the default answering style below. Each call has this system message,
the accumulated user-question/assistant-answer history, and the current question as a new user message.
The returned answer is appended to that history. The two knowledge fields are the initial request and
complete business information; clarification annotations and evaluator code are not included. The retained
implementation requests at most 10,000 output tokens per call and leaves temperature and seed unset.
Customer system prompt (English translation)
You are the person responsible for this business scenario, answering the technical team’s clarification questions
about the requirements.
The following is your business knowledge. Before answering, read each block in full and cross-check them. In
particular, <information> often contains specific values, field names, coordinates, thresholds, and constraint
details. When asked about a schema, parameter, threshold, coordinate, formula, or similar detail, first look
for the existing answer in <information>; do not say "I will provide it" or decide it on the spot:
<instruction>
{{instruction}}
</instruction>
<information>
{{information}}
</information>
Note: Any of the above may contain internal technical details such as evaluation formulas, scoring weights, or
penalty coefficients. Do not volunteer these to the technical team. If asked, you may provide a qualitative
business-level explanation, but do not give specific mathematical formulas or numerical weights.
Mandatory answering procedure (follow these three steps for every question):
Step 1: Check information first (internally; do not include this step in the reply).
Before selecting or writing an answer, find the corresponding text in <information> and answer on that basis.
You are playing the business owner: this is business knowledge in your head, not a document you can consult.
Do not say "checking information", "according to the document/materials/instructions", "original excerpt", or
"not found", or imply that you are consulting materials. Answer directly in your own voice.
29


--- Page 30 ---
Customer system prompt (English translation)
(continued)
Step 2: Compare the options with the facts in information.
- If an option exactly matches the facts in information, select it.
- If none of the options exactly matches, select "Other (please describe)" and copy the ranges, values, or field
names from information.
- Only if information does not address the question may you decide based on instruction.
Step 3: Do not replace specific values with vague qualifications.
Do not answer "unrestricted / not counted / unnecessary / flexible / for the model to decide" unless information
explicitly says so. Copy specific values, ranges, and field names from information.
If selecting an option that says "please describe", provide the specific content after the option name. If there is
nothing new to add, select a negative option rather than leaving the description empty.
Answer requirements:
- Speak as the business owner. Give only the answer itself, without explaining the reasoning or repeating the
question.
- If there are multiple questions, answer each directly on a separate line.
- Do not volunteer implementation details such as evaluation methods, scoring formulas, or exact objective
weights. If asked, you may give a qualitative business-level explanation, but not specific mathematical
formulas or numerical weights.
- If none of the information sources covers the question, provide a reasonable business default.
This prompt allows business defaults for unsupported questions, so answers are not guaranteed to follow from
the case information (Appendix A.8).
A.9.3 Question and answer interfaces
The harness supports native question requests, a scaffold callback, and text exchanges. These routes share
the customer above but preserve each scaffold’s interaction mechanism. The following examples illustrate the
message shapes; angle-bracket values are placeholders, not recorded dialogue.
OpenCode native question tool.
The harness receives a request containing a questions array and replies
through POST /question/<request-id>/reply (or the corresponding session-scoped route in the older API).
Each answer is a one-element string array, preserving free-text answers rather than forcing them into an
agent-proposed option. The customer receives each question string, falling back to header if it is empty;
option metadata is recorded but is not separately appended to that string.
Native question request and reply
Request:
{"id": "<request-id>", "questions": [
{"question": "<question text>", "header": "<short header>",
"options": [{"label": "<option>", "description": "<meaning>"}]}
]}
Reply:
{"answers": [["<customer answer>"]]}
Text exchange and OpenHands callback.
The CLI configurations use text exchanges. OpenHands
obtains a reply via its user-response callback, connected to the customer by the harness. Questions under the
suggested heading are parsed directly when possible; otherwise a detector determines whether the message
requests information. Each detected question is answered separately, and the answers return as one user
message in the form below. Recorded question units used for scoring may be split further as described in
Appendix A.3.
30


--- Page 31 ---
Text-channel request and response
Agent message:
## Questions for the client
<question 1>
<question 2>
Customer reply delivered as a user message:
- <question 1>
<answer 1>
- <question 2>
<answer 2>
The detector sees only agent text, not hidden requirements, and is skipped when the question heading is
present. Replies without a question mark are treated as non-questions; otherwise five models vote by strict
majority of returned ballots on whether the agent is asking. Overlong replies keep the first 2,000 and last
8,000 characters.
Question detector system message
You judge whether a coding agent’s reply is ASKING the client for information, or REPORTING/DELIVERING
work.
Return JSON only:
{"asking": true|false, "questions": ["...", "..."]}
Rules:
- "asking" is true only if the agent is waiting for the client to supply
information it cannot determine itself.
- Rhetorical questions inside an explanation or report are NOT asking.
("How do we balance time against fairness? We weight them 1:90." -> false)
- Offers to continue are NOT asking. ("Shall I also plot the routes?" -> false)
- Split compound questions into atomic ones, one fact per entry.
("What speed, and is loading time included?" -> two entries)
- Keep each question in its original language, close to the agent’s wording.
- If "asking" is false, "questions" must be [].
Question detector user message
Agent reply:
{{clipped_agent_reply}}{{hint}}
The detector requests at most 2,000 output tokens. On malformed JSON it retries once, prepending the
following text to the original user message:
Question detector JSON-repair retry prefix
Your previous response violated the JSON protocol (ValueError). Return exactly one JSON object with keys
asking and questions, and no other text.

The retained text loop sends the following continuation when an agent has stopped without a deliverable,
subject to its run budget, and allows up to three such pushes in that branch. Repeated identical question
batches or exhausted clarification limits also trigger a transition to solving.
Continuation and budget messages
Continuation:
Understood. Please now carry out the work and write the deliverable files into the working directory.
Text-channel clarification budget exhausted:
(No further questions can be answered. Proceed with your best judgement.)
Native-tool / callback clarification budget exhausted:
No further information is available. Proceed with your best judgement.
If a customer call fails, the OpenCode handler returns a placeholder telling the agent to proceed on its own
judgment.
A.9.4 Artifact-extraction instructions
The extractor runs after the solving agent has finished. The shared prompt below inserts the case’s complete
submission_schema.json under Target schema (authoritative). If that file is absent, it uses the evaluator’s
EXTRACTOR_SPEC documentation, or directs the extractor to infer the schema from evaluator source.
Paths identify the retained agent workspace, case data, evaluator, and a separate normalized-output directory.
Shared extractor template
You are a data extractor for a benchmark evaluation pipeline.
## Your task
1. **Read ‘_agent_summary.md‘ first** (if present in the workspace). It tells you which file
the agent considers its final answer. The agent’s own designation decides which artifact
gets graded -- you do not get to pick a different (better-scoring) one.
2. Read the target schema below to learn what files and fields the evaluator accepts.
3. Find the agent’s output in the workspace. Filenames and column names will differ.
4. Normalize it to the schema and write the result to the OUTPUT directory.
5. **If the deliverable is executable code** (the schema asks for a ‘.py‘ defining a specific
function or class): the evaluator imports it from the OUTPUT directory, so copy the entry
file under the required name AND every workspace-local module it imports, directly or
transitively. Copying only the entry file leaves it orphaned -- ModuleNotFoundError, and a
working solution scores 0.
6. Write ‘_result.json‘ to the OUTPUT directory as your final action.
{{schema_block}}
{{verification_block}}
**Stop as soon as the evaluator returns a score.** A 0 is a legitimate final answer: the
agent’s solution ran and did not meet the constraints. Never edit values, add rows, drop
rows, or swap in a different solution file to raise the number. You normalize
*representation* -- filenames, column names, layout, encoding. The decisions are the agent’s
and must survive unchanged. If no score can be obtained, the artifact is wrong; say so and
stop rather than making something up.
**Forbidden transformations.** The following transformations would change the
agent’s substantive answer and are therefore forbidden.
32


--- Page 33 ---
Shared extractor template
(continued)
1. **Nudging values inside a stated tolerance.** Do not adjust a number within an evaluator
tolerance (or any other slack) so that a failing constraint passes. Tolerance exists to
absorb *the agent’s* rounding, not to give the extractor a search space. If the agent’s
numbers land outside a limit, that is the answer: report the 0.
2. **Writing an adapter when the agent’s interface does not match the evaluator’s.** When a
deliverable is code and its signature or data model disagrees with what the evaluator
passes in (e.g. the policy expects a custom object, the evaluator hands it a dict), do
**not** author a shim, a wrapper class, or a re-implementation. Copy the agent’s file
as-is, let it fail, and record the mismatch in ‘notes‘.
3. **Dropping rows that "look wrong".** Removing rows the agent emitted -- even ones that
seem like annotations, placeholders, or infeasible leftovers -- changes the answer. If you
drop or add **any** row, state the before/after counts and the reason in ‘notes‘.
4. **"Fixing" an identifier the agent spelled wrong.** Whether you may repair a bad name
depends on one question: **does the task specify the naming?**
- **Task is silent on naming** (e.g. the agent labels a plate ‘plate1‘ where the evaluator
keys on ‘P001‘): map it, provided the target is **unique** in the reference data. This
is ordinary identifier normalization. If the mapping is ambiguous or has no match,
do not guess -- leave it and say so.
- **Task states the naming rule** (e.g. ‘information.md‘ says feature names must be
real columns of the training data, in ‘{trait}_D{day}‘ form): a name that breaks the
rule is a **substantive error by the agent**, not a formatting slip. Copy it as-is and
let it score 0.
Check ‘information.md‘ / ‘instruction.md‘ for a naming rule **before** you repair any
name. Also check the schema’s ‘role‘: repairing is only ever in scope for ‘identifier‘
fields, never for ‘decision‘ fields -- those are the answer itself.
5. **Using the evaluator’s own formula to generate a value the evaluator checks.** When the
schema documents how a field relates to others (‘sub_i_long must equal
mother_cut_weight / (mother_width x 7.65) x 10000‘), that formula is there so you can
understand the field -- **not so you can compute it**. Filling the field from the formula
makes the consistency check pass by construction: the evaluator ends up verifying its own
arithmetic instead of the agent’s. A derived value that the evaluator validates is
load-bearing even when it is not itself a decision variable.
The test is not "is this field a decision?" -- it is **"does the evaluator look at it?"**
If yes, the value must come from the agent, even when you can compute a better one, and
even when the agent’s is provably inconsistent. An inconsistency you found is a finding to
report in ‘notes‘, not a defect to repair.
## When the agent’s designated file is incomplete
Rule 1 says the agent’s own designation decides what gets graded. That assumes the
designated artifact exists and is coherent. When it is **not**:
- **The designation names a state the agent never finished.** If the designated artifact is
incomplete or internally contradictory, fall back to the most recent complete state that
passes the agent’s own validation, set ‘status‘ to ‘partial‘, and say in ‘notes‘ which state
you used and why the designated one was left out. This is not "picking the better-scoring
file" -- it is selecting the only file that is a coherent answer.
- **Extra rows beyond the graded set.** Rows the agent produced for keys that are not in the
evaluation set should be dropped, with the before/after counts disclosed. That is different
from dropping rows the agent *did* produce for graded keys, which is forbidden.
## Verify order-bearing fields before you write
When a field encodes a sequence (a visit order, a permutation, or a concatenated route), its
order **is** the decision. Reconstructing it from a grouped source can silently scramble the
group order even when all members and counts match.
33


--- Page 34 ---
Shared extractor template
(continued)
Before writing an order-bearing field, re-derive it from the source a second way and compare
element by element. If the schema gives you a companion structure (a ‘trips‘ array with per-
trip stop counts, say), slice your sequence by those counts and check each slice against the
source group it should match.
Rule of thumb: if an edit would change the score, it is not normalization. Reformatting,
renaming, reshaping, re-encoding never change a score -- those are yours to make freely.
## Normalization rules
- **Semantic-first mapping**: the same column name does not guarantee the same meaning.
Check the schema’s field definition (units, scope, total vs. net) before renaming.
- **Column renaming / format conversion**: fuzzy-match agent columns to schema fields;
convert wide/long layouts as needed.
- **Missing rows**: only fill a missing combination with zero when the schema defines that
dimension’s absence AS zero. Do NOT invent rows for tasks the agent did not produce --
leave them out and set status to "partial".
- **Never** re-run the agent’s solver, re-optimize, or re-compute its decisions.
- **Prefer the highest-precision artifact.** When the agent expresses the same decisions in
several files -- say a minute-truncated CSV and a full-precision JSON -- take the lossless
one, even if ‘_agent_summary.md‘ names the other. Precision loss is not a formatting
choice; it silently changes the answer being graded.
- **Never take anything from the Data directory as the agent’s output.** ‘data/‘ holds the
problem input, including any baseline or seed policy shipped with the task. Submitting one
of those grades the benchmark’s own reference instead of the agent -- if the workspace has
no real deliverable, say so and set status to "failed".
## Paths & permissions
| Directory | Path | Read | Write |
|-----------|------|------|-------|
| Workspace | ‘{{workspace}}‘ | YES | **NO** |
| Data
| ‘{{data_dir}}‘ | YES | **NO** |
| Evaluator | ‘{{evaluator}}‘ | YES | **NO** |
| Output
| ‘{{output_dir}}‘ | YES | **YES** |
All writes go to the Output directory only.
## _result.json format
{
"status": "success",
"notes": "what was found and what transformations were applied",
"files_found": ["relative paths of agent output files discovered"],
"files_normalized": ["filenames written to the output directory (excluding _result.json)"]
}
Status: "success" = all required files written; "partial" = found output but it is
incomplete or self-contradictory (describe what is missing); "failed" = no relevant agent
output found. When the agent’s output is genuinely incomplete, "partial" is the correct
outcome -- do NOT reconstruct or re-solve to reach "success".
The verification_block uses the first block below for ordinary cases. Case 13, whose evaluator launches
expensive solver subprocesses, uses the second block and is scored after the extractor exits.
34


--- Page 35 ---
Standard extractor verification block
## Verify by running the evaluator (required)
A schema cannot enumerate every shape an agent might produce, so do not guess whether your
normalization is right -- check it:
‘‘‘bash
python3 {{evaluator}} --data-dir {{data_dir}} --submission-dir {{output_dir}}
‘‘‘
React to *structural* failures only:
| What you see | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| ‘ModuleNotFoundError‘ | a module the entry file imports is missing | copy that module in too |
| ‘AttributeError: must define <fn>‘ | wrong entry file | try the next candidate |
| ‘missing <file>‘ / ‘KeyError‘ / missing column | filename or column mapping is off | fix the mapping |
| valid JSON with any score, **including 0** | the evaluator ran to completion | **stop -- you are done** |
Executable-case verification exception (case 13)
## Heavyweight executable case
Do not run ‘{{evaluator}}‘ or the Agent solver. Copy the selected Agent Python
source byte-for-byte to the required output filename. Do not rewrite its CLI,
output shape, algorithm, or decisions: incompatibility is an Agent result.
The scoring stage evaluates it after you exit.
The extractor’s status describes the extraction only; the evaluator alone scores the artifact (Appendix A.3).
A.9.5 Clarification-coverage judge messages
Each judge receives the same system message and, for each registered requirement, the user template below.
The numbered question list is the complete run-level list after splitting. Calls use temperature zero.
Coverage judge system message
You grade whether an agent’s clarification questions uncovered a specific hidden requirement. Judge strictly and
reply with JSON only.
Coverage judge user message
A client holds the hidden requirement below. An agent asked the questions
below to clarify the task. Decide what the client would reveal in reply.
HIDDEN REQUIREMENT (id: {{requirement_id}})
{{requirement_description}}
{{optional_trigger_block}}
AGENT’S QUESTIONS (each on its own line, numbered)
{{numbered_questions}}
The client answers cooperatively and concretely: when a question points at a
35


--- Page 36 ---
Coverage judge user message
(continued)
topic they hold information about, they state the actual values or rules rather
than a generic description. They do NOT volunteer information the agent never
asked about.
Judge two things:
1. ATTEMPTED -- does any question point at this requirement’s topic, however
loosely phrased?
2. COVERED -- answering that question, would the client state the specific
requirement above?
- Yes if the question names the specific quantity, rule, field or entity this
requirement is about, so the client knows exactly which convention to state.
The agent need not already know the value, nor use the same wording; asking
what the convention is counts.
- No if the question merely names a topic, module or data source and asks what
to "watch out for", what the "rules" are, or what is "special" -- even when
that topic is the right one. Such a question does not tell the client which
of the many conventions in that area is wanted, so a cooperative client
would ask back rather than recite this requirement.
Examples that must be judged No: "anything special about the data?",
"any rules I should know about billing?", "any pitfalls when reading these
sheets?". Naming the right domain does not make a question specific.
Reply with JSON only:
{"attempted": true|false, "covered": true|false,
"question_indices": [<1-based indices that cover it>]}
Optional trigger-example block
QUESTIONS THAT WOULD SURFACE IT (reference examples, not exhaustive --
a differently-worded question that targets the same fact also counts)
{{indented_trigger_bullets}}

with the prefix below.
